historical: Before a people can keep accounts, treaties or spellbooks, they must first agree that a mark on clay can stand for a sound. The alphabet is the quiet invention on which every later one rests.
The oldest reading of the world: that the river, the stone and the storm each carry a will of their own. Animist shamans do not command nature so much as negotiate with it.
The craft of binding a spell into a made thing, so that the enchantment outlives the enchanter. An artificer's blade remembers its instructions long after the hand that forged it is dust.
The first systematic attempt to read the future in the fixed order of the sky. Its charts were wrong about destiny and right about the calendar, which proved the more useful gift.
A river is a wall until someone learns to span it. Bridge building turns a frontier into a road and a besieged province into a supplied one.
Laying out the dead with intent is the first evidence anywhere of a people who believe in something beyond the day. Every temple in history descends from a grave dug carefully.
The first initiation into chaos: the student learns that fire answers willingly and obeys badly. Adepts are recognised less by their skill than by their scars.
The collected findings of wizards who studied disorder itself, and the smaller collection of those who survived doing so.
A chaos mage no longer coaxes the flame but argues with it, and usually wins. The distinction matters to everyone standing nearby.
The discipline of drawing power from the raw unmade, where nothing is stable and therefore nothing is forbidden. Its practitioners trade safety for reach.
Mastery of chaos is not control; it is the ability to stand at the centre of something uncontrolled and remain intact.
At the wizard's grade, chaos is no longer a force to be handled but a country to be travelled. Few return unchanged, and fewer return unwilling to go back.
A code invented to make heavily armed men on expensive horses tolerable to the people who fed them. It worked well enough to outlive its own cavalry.
The moment a ruling is written down, it stops belonging to the ruler. Written law is the first real limit any sovereign ever accepted.
Stone laid to a plan rather than to a habit. Construction is what separates a settlement that endures a siege from one that endures a season.
A token everyone agrees is worth something becomes worth something. Currency lets a farmer trade with a shipwright who does not want grain.
The novice necromancer learns the least popular truth in magic: that the dead are a resource, and an obedient one.
Accumulated study of the boundary between living and not, compiled by scholars whom no city willingly houses.
A death mage commands what was once a person. The price of that power is that no one will ever again sit comfortably beside them.
The art of reaching past the end of a life and finding that something still answers. Universally condemned, and widely practised in wartime.
To master death magic is to stand, for practical purposes, outside the ordinary account of who owes what to whom.
The death wizard has stopped negotiating with mortality and started administering it.
Knowledge that predates the peoples who study it, recovered in fragments from places better left unexcavated.
The recognition that wind, tide and season are not moods but mechanisms, and that a mechanism can be driven.
Whatever comes after the last thing anyone thought to name. Every age has believed it had reached this point.
Marks that hold power rather than meaning. A glyph carved correctly will still be working when no one alive can read it.
The final grade, at which a wizard's limitation is no longer knowledge or power but judgement.
Workings laid not on an object or a person but on a place, a season, or an army. Their scale is what makes them greater and what makes them dangerous.
The study of the beasts that were never meant to be catalogued: the ones with opinions, wings, or both.
The oldest use anyone ever found for power, and still the one that buys the most loyalty.
Soldiers who fight because they are certain rather than because they are paid. History records both how effective and how unmanageable this is.
The discovery that men will follow a person further than they will follow an order.
Small, durable workings: a blade that will not dull, a granary that will not spoil. Unglamorous magic that quietly wins wars.
Careful observation of ordinary animals, which turns out to be the necessary apprenticeship for handling the extraordinary ones.
The first lessons in the magic of vitality, taught almost everywhere and mastered almost nowhere.
The gathered record of what can be mended, what can be strengthened, and what should be left exactly as it is.
A life mage can return a dying soldier to the line. Armies grasped the strategic implications of this faster than priests grasped the moral ones.
Power drawn from growth and continuation rather than from force. The slowest school to show results and the hardest to break.
At mastery, the life mage's difficulty is no longer healing the wounded but deciding whom not to heal.
The life wizard treats mortality as a condition rather than as a verdict.
Writing lets one generation argue with the next. Every institution that outlasts its founder depends on it.
A map is a claim about the world made portable. Empires have been won by the side with the better one.
The discipline of being certain about something you cannot see. Everything from taxation to ballistics follows from it.
The art of changing what a thing fundamentally is, rather than merely how it behaves. Reversal is not guaranteed.
The conviction that the world has an inside, and the various disciplines invented to get at it.
An apprenticeship spent outdoors, learning that the natural world cooperates only with those who have been asking politely for years.
The collected knowledge of growing things, weather and beasts, held mostly by people who distrust cities.

A nature mage does not defeat the land; they recruit it. Every tradition that worked this way treated weather, beasts and growing things as allies to be bargained with rather than obstacles to be overcome.
Power borrowed from living systems, on the strict understanding that it is a loan.
Mastery here looks like nothing happening: the storm that did not come, the famine that did not arrive.
The nature wizard is answerable to the land, and the arrangement is genuinely mutual.
Finding a destination out of sight of land. The technique is unremarkable; the nerve it required was not.
Formal, sceptical investigation of the hidden, undertaken by scholars who mostly wished the results had come back negative.
The doctrine that divinity is distributed rather than located. Convenient for empires with many conquered gods to absorb.
A fired clay jar is a solved problem in storage, and storage is what lets a people survive a bad year.
The applied science of controlled fire, developed by people who mostly wanted a better festival and accidentally armed everyone.
Runes bind meaning into shape. Carved into a weapon or a wall, they hold their instruction indefinitely and without supervision.
Moving waste away from drinking water has saved more lives than every physician in history combined.
The decision to treat the sea as a road rather than as an edge.
What sailors know that charts do not record: currents, tempers, and which waters have something living under them.
Command of the deep water, which historically has meant command of everything the deep water touches.
The first professional intermediaries between a people and whatever they believed was listening.
The theoretical backbone of sorcery, written down by practitioners who wanted successors rather than rivals.
The disciplined manipulation of force at a distance. Less spectacular than chaos, and considerably more reliable.
The adept's year is spent on precision, because sorcery punishes approximation immediately.
A sorcery mage does openly and instantly what an engineer would need a season and a workforce to accomplish.
Mastery of sorcery is measured in restraint, since by this grade the capability is no longer in question.
The sorcery wizard treats the laws of the world as defaults rather than as limits.
The realisation that where soldiers stand matters more than how many of them there are.
The formal study of wonder-working: taking the miracle apart to see whether it can be repeated on demand.
The proposition that authority can be lent out and taken back. Radical, fragile, and repeatedly rediscovered.
An institution built on the assumption that knowledge should outlive the knowledgeable.
The rules fighting men impose on themselves, which are what distinguish an army from a mob with weapons.
The systematisation of magic into something that can be taught, examined and graded: the moment power became a profession.
Cities die of thirst long before they die of siege. The aqueduct is the unglamorous engineering that lets a town become a city at all.
Housing soldiers together turns them from armed men into a unit. Barracks are where drill, discipline and the habit of obedience are manufactured.
A tower kept lit by scholars rather than sailors, signalling that this city will pay for knowledge and protect those who bring it.
Built to be larger than any need it served, on the correct assumption that awe is a form of civic order.
The oldest declaration a settlement can make: that it intends to still be here next year.
Guns and wards facing the water, built by every port that has been raided exactly once.
A crowd that is entertained is a crowd that is not rioting. Rulers understood this long before they admitted it.
Where a grievance goes instead of a feud. The courthouse is how a distant capital is felt in a provincial street.
Stalls built to hold things that resent being held. The stablemasters here are paid hazard rates and earn them.
Storing the good harvest against the bad one is the single decision that separates a people who persist from a people who scatter.
A sheltered place to unload. Everything a coastal city becomes, it becomes because of this.
A room where the dead are still arguing. Cities that keep one compound their advantages; cities that burn one start over.
An organised body of engineers who guard their methods jealously and sell their results dearly.
Traders who discovered that acting together beats competing, and who quietly became a second government in many cities.
More than a harbour: warehousing, customs, and the machinery of turning a shoreline into an economy.
A place where the raw stuff of magic surfaces of its own accord. Cities are not built near these by accident.
The first public building any people erect, and usually the last one they will consent to see torn down.
Teaching and disputation under one roof, chartered so that neither crown nor church can quite shut it.
Part citadel, part laboratory. Its walls are built to keep things in as much as to keep armies out.
Falling water put to work at scale, trading a valley for a supply of power that never has to be mined.
Concentrated industrial power, bought at a cost the surrounding air and water pay on the city's behalf.
Where the songs are written that decide how a war will be remembered. Rulers who ignored the bards were forgotten by them.
A light raised to be seen from outside the world, on the theory that something out there is watching and can be signalled.
A school built over a site nobody sane would choose, precisely because what leaks out of it is worth studying.
The perfected draught that changes the drinker into whatever the maker intended. The making took generations; the drinking takes a moment.
A cave the land itself has enchanted, tended rather than built. Its keepers claim, plausibly, that it predates them.
A machine that runs on things falling apart, which is the one fuel supply that can never be exhausted.
A spring that will not run dry and a field that will not fail. Every famine legend in the world is a story about looking for this.
A smithy where the metal argues back. What comes out is never quite what was ordered and is often better.
The formal recognition that the land is a party to the bargain, and the place where that bargain is renewed.
Vaults dug by people who consider accounting a sacred discipline and interest a form of poetry.
The attempt to gather everything anyone knows into one building. Every civilisation tries it once, and its loss is always the age's defining wound.
Where heroes are registered, outfitted and, when necessary, invented. The paperwork is more of the legend than anyone admits.
One expedition that went further than was reasonable and came back with a map that redrew everyone's world.
An agreement among people who did not want to be governed, to be governed slightly, mostly regarding each other.
A tower devoted to the study of influence: what a mind will accept if it is approached in the right order.
Raised by an adept who left no name, only instructions. The instructions are still being followed.
An institution built on ambiguous answers, which survived because ambiguous answers are never wrong.
A monument to the argument that a contented population is cheaper to rule than a frightened one.
A garden, a library and a workshop kept by one scholar in exile, who proved that isolation and mastery are related.
A single finding that reorganised an entire discipline, and made its discoverer permanently unwelcome in it.
A single carved mark that makes obedience feel like agreement. Its existence is the strongest argument ever made against runes.
Proportion made permanent. Built as a temple, remembered as a definition of how a building should be.
A rampart raised from the fallen, which defends a city and also reminds it, daily, of what defence has cost.
The organised decision to leave the world entirely, undertaken for reasons that were half curiosity and half rivalry.
The end of one of the oldest quiet arithmetics of human life, achieved not by a genius but by an institution that refused to stop.
A fire kept burning so that strangers can find the harbour. One of the few monuments built entirely for other people's benefit.
A figure raised at a harbour mouth to state a proposition, addressed to arrivals rather than to residents.
The extension of the vote to half the population, resisted for a century on grounds nobody can now restate without embarrassment.
Rotation, drainage and selected seed. Nothing about it looks impressive, and it doubles what a valley can feed.
Deep shafts, pumps and timbering: the difference between scraping a hillside and genuinely working it.
Deliberate planting in worked ground. The first improvement any people ever make to the land, and the one everything else waits on.
Earth and stone arranged so that attacking costs more than defending. The whole of siege history is an argument with this.
Taking metal and stone out of the ground on purpose. Hard, short-lived work that every army in history has depended on.
Ground formally set aside from use. A late idea, and one that only occurs to peoples who have already used up somewhere else.
Fixed fishing works in shallow water: a harvest that arrives without being planted.
Iron road and a machine that never tires. It collapsed distance more sharply than any invention before it.
A prepared surface between two places. Trade, tax collection and armies all move at the speed of the worst road on the route.
What is left where someone else tried this. Ruins are a warning and, to the right visitor, an inheritance.
Reshaping ground into arid upland, undertaken where the alternative was worse.
Raising barren peaks by will rather than by geology, an act of engineering that reads as an act of vandalism.
Deliberately drying a region. Almost always done to deny it to someone else.
Planting a forest where there was none and waiting, or refusing to wait and compelling it.
Turning difficult ground into pasture and field, the single most common ambition of every settled people.
Raising ground for the sake of the defensive advantage and the drainage that come with it.
Encouraging dense growth, usually as a barrier, occasionally out of conviction.
Making mountains. The most expensive way ever devised to build a wall.
Flattening and clearing into open country: easy to farm, easy to cross, easy to invade.
Deliberate flooding. Miserable to hold, and historically very effective at stopping cavalry.
Raising frozen upland, generally at the edges of a realm that has run out of better land.
Ice-locked peaks made to order, the harshest terrain anyone has bothered to manufacture.
A shed, a scale and an agreed price, at the point where two peoples find it easier to deal than to raid.
The claim that the means of production should be held in common, and the long argument about who holds them on everyone's behalf.
A state whose sovereignty is exercised through chartered companies, in which citizenship and shareholding become difficult to distinguish.
Rule by the governed, accepted slowly and everywhere on the grounds that every alternative had been tried first.
A polity that treats the land as a constituency with standing, and accepts a lower ceiling in exchange for a longer horizon.
The subordination of everything to the state, sold as unity and delivered as obedience.
One family, one claim, and an inheritance treated as a constitution. Stable while the heirs are competent.
Rule by those who can demonstrate expertise, which works until the question at hand is not a technical one.
Continuous consent, gathered instantly and constantly. It removes the delay between opinion and policy, along with the reflection that lived in it.

gameplay: The opening age. Research is cheap and slow, cities are small, and almost every advance you take opens two more. Expansion now compounds for the rest of the game.
The second age. Writing, law and organised warfare arrive together; cities begin to support specialists, and the first wonders become buildable.
The age of walls, guilds and cavalry. Defensive improvements outpace attack, so wars become sieges and economies become the deciding factor.
Science accelerates sharply and the map opens up. Advances arrive faster than governments adapt to them, which is what makes this age volatile.
Production dominates. Output per city climbs steeply, and pollution and unhappiness become live constraints rather than background noise.
Information becomes the limiting resource. Science and commerce multipliers matter more than raw production, and stealth and espionage units come into their own.
Late-game engineering. Terraforming, extreme improvements and the most expensive wonders in the game all become reachable here.
The final age. The advance tree is effectively exhausted and further research yields incremental Future Technology rather than new capabilities.

historical: The idea that a defender should not merely absorb an attack but answer it. Fortifications that shoot back are older than fortifications that do not.
Knowledge accumulates in one direction only. What one generation discovers, the next assumes, which is why progress feels slow while it is happening and inevitable afterwards.
Two powers agreeing that a third is the more urgent problem. Most alliances outlive their reason for existing by exactly one war.
Acts that even warring peoples agree lie outside war. The category exists because it has repeatedly needed to be named.
The word every settled people uses for the peoples outside their walls. It says more about the speaker than the subject.
The decision to stop building things and simply take the money instead. A mature economy's admission that gold is more flexible than stone.
A settlement large enough that most of its inhabitants do not grow their own food. Every consequence of civilisation follows from that one fact.
Exchange between strangers, conducted on trust in a system rather than trust in a person. The whole of urban wealth rests on it.
What happens in the gap between what a state forbids and what it can observe. The gap widens with distance from the capital.
The older and cheaper half of warfare. It is generally underfunded in peace and frantically overfunded the season after a raid.
The practice of getting what an army would take, without the army. Cheaper, slower, and reversible.
Unmaking a settlement deliberately. Rare, drastic, and almost always a decision about a frontier that could not be held.
War conducted through the ledger. It hurts slowly, indiscriminately, and often the wrong people.
Every realm has a distance beyond which orders arrive late and taxes arrive short. Empires do not usually fall; they exceed this radius.
The first constraint and the last one. No policy, army or wonder survives a people that is not eating.
Stored, portable agreement. Its usefulness is that it can become almost anything else on short notice.
Things worth carrying a long way, which is a much shorter list than things worth having.
The arrangement a people accepts for deciding who may compel whom. Every form is a different trade between order and consent.
Populations expand to whatever their food, water and patience allow. Managing that ceiling is most of what governing a city is.
The measure of whether a population consents to be governed. It is cheap to maintain and enormously expensive to restore.
Permanent works inside a city that change what it is capable of. Their cost is paid once and their upkeep forever.
The works nobody notices until they fail: roads, drains, aqueducts, walls. Civilisation is largely maintenance.
Everything built must be kept. The standing cost of past decisions is what constrains present ones.
How much of a realm's substance is committed to the possibility of war. Too little invites it; too much causes it.
A proposal made in the expectation of refusal, so that the refusal can be pointed to later.
Past a certain density, adding people subtracts from everyone. Cities discover this threshold by crossing it.
The cost of production that is paid by whoever lives downstream, which is why it took so long to be counted at all.
The one resource that produces every other one, and the only one with an opinion about how it is used.
Labour turned into things. The rate at which a realm can convert intent into fact.
Effort spent on the land rather than in the city: roads, farms, mines. Slow to pay back and impossible to do without.
Deciding how much a population eats is the bluntest instrument a government has, and the one most likely to end it.
What one power privately thinks of another, which governs everything it will do before it says anything.
Asking, in circumstances where both parties understand what follows a refusal.
The moment a population stops believing its government is inevitable. Everything after that is bookkeeping.
Disorder that has stopped being individual. A city in riot is not producing, defending, or listening.
Water, transport, defence and a boundary, all in one line on the map. Nearly every old city sits on one.
The physical evidence that this has all been attempted before, left standing as a matter of indifference rather than respect.
Paying in gold for the time you do not have. Always more expensive than planning, and occasionally worth it.
Organised doubt. Its power comes from being willing to discard its own conclusions, which no other institution manages.
The perennial decision between what a realm knows next year and what it can afford this year.
Settlement of water, undertaken when the land is full or the sea holds something the land does not.
Labour taken rather than bought. It builds quickly, costs continuously, and has never yet failed to be repaid.
Citizens taken off the fields to do one thing extremely well. The surplus that permits this is the definition of wealth.
Small numbers, chosen carefully, sent where an army cannot go and a diplomat will not.
The failure state of every other system, and the one that arrives fastest.
Forces whose advantage is not being seen. Their entire value collapses the moment they are, which makes them expensive to use well.
Standing armies eat in peacetime too. The bill for readiness is paid every turn, in the currency of everything not built instead.
Rebuilding the land itself rather than adapting to it. The last stage of the argument between a people and their geography.
A promise made in the hope of never having to keep it. Its whole value lies in being believed, which is why a threat that is tested once is rarely worth making twice.
Work done to the ground outside the walls, which is where a city's food, metal and roads actually come from.
How a thing is said, which between powers is frequently more consequential than what is said.
The discovery that both sides can end an exchange better off. Every peace that has ever lasted has been built on it.
A path along which goods move reliably enough to plan around. Protecting one is the commonest reason for a war nobody wanted.
Written agreements between powers that recognise no higher authority, and are therefore held together by nothing but interest.
An organised body of people acting as one. The basic instrument by which a realm applies force to the map.
Soldiers who have survived. What they know cannot be trained into recruits, only inherited from them.
Winning by leaving no one else standing. The oldest definition, and the only one that requires no agreement.
Winning by being the power everyone else prefers. Slower than conquest and considerably harder to reverse.
Judgement by accumulated account at a fixed date, which rewards steadiness over any single decisive stroke.
Winning by understanding the world first, on the assumption that understanding is a lead nobody else can close.
What a realm can actually see. Every decision is made about the map as known, not the map as it is.
What a state pays its own people to remain its own people. Set it too low and the labour leaves; set it too high and there is nothing left to govern with.
Works so large that only one of each can exist. They are built for the advantage and remembered for the ambition.
The person doing the work. Every abstraction on this page resolves, eventually, to them.
How hard a population is asked to labour. Push it up and output rises, then consent falls, in that order.
Removing one person instead of an army. Cheap, deniable, and historically far less decisive than the people who order it expect.
The oldest instruction in warfare, and the one every other order exists to make unnecessary or survivable.
Putting an army aboard ship. The most vulnerable hour in any campaign is the one spent doing this.
Striking at range and accepting no reply. It wins ground slowly and costs almost nothing but ammunition and patience.
Changing what a population believes, on the correct assumption that belief decides who they will fight for.
Sending soldiers home. Easy to order and, for many governments, extremely difficult to survive.
A permanent presence in someone else's capital, which is simultaneously a courtesy and a listening post.
Removing a foreign force without killing it, so that a border dispute does not become a war.
Treatment by conviction. It works often enough to be defended and rarely enough to be argued about forever.
Digging in. The single cheapest multiplier a defender has ever had access to.
Persuading a rival's own people to do what an army would otherwise have to. Slow, cheap, and impossible to control once begun.
Turning a subject population against its occupier, which is easier to start than any commander has ever found it to stop.
Buying contentment outright. It works immediately, and teaches the population exactly what discontent is worth.
Taking a rival's commerce rather than their territory. Less glorious, and generally more damaging.
Finding out what is actually inside the walls before deciding whether to knock on them.
Placing troops behind a line instead of through it. Everything depends on what arrives with them, which is usually not enough.
Destroying what cannot be taken. It denies a rival their improvements and guarantees the ground is worthless to whoever holds it next.
Deliberate contagion, the one weapon in history that has reliably come home to the side that used it.
Hitting the enemy from outside the reach of their answer, which has been the central ambition of weapon design ever since the sling.
Changing a system from inside it, at the pace the system permits, which is the whole difficulty.
Founding a city. The single most consequential act any group of people can perform on a map.
Taking people as property. It supplies labour immediately and creates an enemy permanently.
Standing down until needed. Armies spend the overwhelming majority of their existence in this state.
Announcing the future with enough authority that people begin arranging their affairs around it.
Acquiring in one night what a rival spent a generation learning. The cheapest research any realm has ever conducted.
Public generosity as policy. Rulers who understood this outlasted rulers who considered it beneath them.
A route maintained by people with no authority, for people with no options, against a law everyone involved considers illegitimate.
Putting an army ashore. The moment a naval campaign becomes a land one.
Re-equipping veterans rather than replacing them, which keeps the one thing that cannot be manufactured: experience.
Dry, broken upland where the soil has already left. Peoples settle it for what it overlooks rather than for what it grows.
Bare rock in a dead range, holding neither snow nor forest. Its only exports have ever been ore and distance.
Ground that has been used up, poisoned or cursed past the point where anything returns to it. Every civilisation eventually makes some.
Land defined by what it lacks. It has been crossed by every trading people in history and settled by very few of them.
The reason a caravan route runs where it does. Deserts hold their few valuable things where nobody would look without a guide.
A find worth the journey across dry country, which is the only justification anyone has ever needed for the journey.
Timber, game and cover. Forests fed the shipwrights and hid the armies, and were felled by both.
What the woods yield to those who know them, and withhold entirely from those who do not.
A second gift of the deep woods, generally found by the people who live in them rather than by the people who claim them.
Ice deep enough to have its own geography. It moves, slowly, and rearranges everything it passes over.
Open, watered, level ground. Nearly every people who settled permanently did so on it, and nearly every war was about who would.
A staple crop that turns good land into crowded land. Populations rise to meet it within a generation.
High enough to see from and to hold, low enough to farm. Fortresses cluster on hills for a reason older than any of them.
Something worth digging for under rising ground, which is where most of the world's metal has always come from.
A resource of the uplands, valuable enough that the people below have repeatedly come up for it.
Dense, wet and hostile to everything with wheels. It is crossed rarely and controlled almost never.
What grows in the deep green that grows nowhere else, and has therefore always been worth an expedition.
The oldest border there is. Mountains divide peoples more reliably than any treaty and require no enforcement.
Open ground, easily farmed and easily ridden across. Its history is one of prosperity punctuated by cavalry.
A prize of the open country, which is difficult to defend precisely because it is easy to reach.
Water that has not decided to be a lake. Miserable to live in, and historically excellent at stopping armies.
Something valuable in the wet ground, recovered by people willing to accept the fever that comes with it.
The marsh's compensation for everything else about the marsh.
Frozen a hand's depth down all year. It supports herds, herders, and almost nothing that stays put.
Where the sea gives ground. Every landing, every port and every invasion in history has begun on one.
Open ocean, out of sight of everything. It was the last part of the world to be mapped and the first to be feared.
Underwater forest, sheltering the fish that feed the coast. Its value was understood by fishermen centuries before naturalists.
Living stone just under the surface. It builds the richest waters anywhere and sinks the ships that come to use them.
A tear in the sea floor where heat comes up from below. Whatever lives down there evolved without reference to the sun.
Water a person can stand in. The whole of coastal fishing, and most of coastal defence, happens here.
The drowned edge of the land, shallow enough to work and rich enough to be worth fighting over.
A yield of the continental shelf, reachable by any fleet with the patience to look for it.
What the shallow banks give up to anyone who has learned where the banks are.
A second harvest of the shelf, and a common reason for two coastal peoples to discover they disagree about borders.
A mountain building itself out of the sea, one eruption at a time. New land, arriving violently.
Snow-covered upland, held mostly by people who were pushed there and stayed out of stubbornness.
Peaks under permanent ice. They are crossed by perhaps one pass, and whoever holds that pass holds the region.
